Appendix A Renormalization of the Entropy

It is well known that the entanglement entropy SoutS_{\text{out}} on one side of a sharp boundary σ\sigma is subject to UV divergences. Thus in order to define the generalized entropy SgenS_{\text{gen}}, we must invoke a renormalization procedure. We start by regulating SoutS_{\text{out}} using a UV cutoff associated with some distance scale ϵ\epsilon, so that the outside entropy Sout(ϵ)S_{\text{out}}^{(\epsilon)} now depends on the regulator. This could be done using e.g. a heat kernel regulator [66, 67], Pauli-Villars [68, 69], a brick wall cutoff [70], the mutual information [71], or a variety of other methods.

The leading-order divergence is proportional to the area [29, 72, 73], but in dimensions D≥4D\geq 4 there are additional subleading divergences, each proportional to some local geometrical integral on the boundary. In dimension DD there are subleading divergent corrections with weight up to DD. Since perturbative quantum gravity is a nonrenormalizable theory, one can also even higher curvature corrections by considering 2-loop or higher diagrams involving gravitons. Higher curvature corrections can also arise from stringy effects.

When calculating the generalized entropy, each of these divergences is absorbed into a counterterm, i.e., a parameter in the gravitational action II which controls the size of a correction to the gravitational entropy SgravS_{\text{grav}}. We shall see that the total quantity Sgen=Sgrav+SoutS_{\text{gen}}=S_{\text{grav}}+S_{\text{out}} is invariant under the RG flow. Thus these counterterms are important part of the definition of the QFC, although they drop out of the QNEC for the reasons described in section 5.2.

A.1 The Replica Trick

The replica trick (reviewed in [74]) is a convenient way to calculate the von Neumann entropy −tr​(ρ​log⁡ρ)-\text{tr}(\rho\log\rho), without the nuisance of taking the logarithm of a matrix. This trick is based on instead evaluating the Renyi entropy

Sn=11−n​ln⁡tr⁡(ρn)S_{n}=\frac{1}{1-n}\ln\mathrm{tr}(\rho^{n}) (50)

and analytically continuing to n=1n=1 to obtain SS. In cases where the state ρ\rho comes from a Euclidean path integral, there is a beautiful geometrical interpretation of the Renyi entropy in terms of an nn-sheeted cover M(n)M^{(n)} of the manifold, having a conical singularity with total angle 2​π​n2\pi n on the entangling surface σ\sigma. Assuming that one can analytically continue the effective action Ieff=−ln⁡ZI_{\mathrm{eff}}=-\ln Z from the positive integers to n=1n=1, one then writes

Sreplica=−(1−n∂n)Ieff|n=1.S_{\text{replica}}=-(1-n\partial_{n})I_{\mathrm{eff}}\Big|_{n=1}. (51)

This defines the geometrical or replica entropy for the state of the quantum fields outside of σ\sigma [30, 26, 75, 76, 31, 77, 78, 79, 80].

Inserting the 1-loop effective action IeffI_{\mathrm{eff}} of a quantum field, we obtain a nonlocal answer for SreplicaS_{\text{replica}}, as expected. However, the UV divergences in IeffI_{\mathrm{eff}} are local, allowing us to compute the corresponding divergences in SreplicaS_{\text{replica}}.

Note that the identification of SreplicaS_{\text{replica}} with the von Neumann entropy SoutS_{\mathrm{out}} is somewhat formal, due to the fact that the replicated manifold has a delta function of curvature at the conical singularity.1414 14 This curvature is sometimes smoothed out slightly in order to evaluate the entropy [81], although this smoothing does not by itself eliminate the UV divergences associated with coupling to the curvature. Matter fields can couple to the curvature at the tip, producing “contact terms” whose interpretation will be discussed in section A.4.

Now nothing stops us from inserting a classical gravitational action I⁡[ga​b]I[g_{ab}] into (51) (treating the n-sheeted cover manifold as a fixed background metric). In this case everything cancels except for a contribution coming from the conical singularity. So in this case we obtain an entropy which is local on σ\sigma, which we call the gravitational entropy SgravS_{\text{grav}}.

If II is the Einstein-Hilbert action, Gibbons and Hawking obtained by this method the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy A/4​G​ℏA/4G\hbar [82], thus explaining why this term is included in the generalized entropy. If on the other hand II is a higher-curvature action, one obtains additional correction terms in SgravS_{\text{grav}}. For the stationary case, in which σ\sigma lies on a Killing horizon, the analytic continuation is easy due to the presence of the rotational symmetry about the bifurcation surface, and hence SgravS_{\text{grav}} is given by the Wald entropy [83, 84, 85, 86], obtained by differentiating the Lagrangian with respect to the Riemann tensor and multiplying by the binormal ϵμ​ν\epsilon_{\mu\nu} twice:

SWald=−2​πℏ∫σd2xg2∂I∂Rμ​ν​ξ​oϵμ​νϵξ​o.S_{\mathrm{Wald}}=-\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\int_{\sigma}d^{2}x\sqrt{{}^{2}g}\frac{\partial I}{\partial R_{\mu\nu\xi o}}\epsilon_{\mu\nu}\epsilon_{\xi o}. (52)

However, Wald’s Noether charge method for deriving the entropy is subject to ambiguities for non-stationary horizons [84, 85], and is therefore unable to determine the coefficients of those terms which vanish on stationary horizons, e.g. terms involving products of extrinsic curvatures.

Thus, for the nonstationary case, there are additional corrections to the Wald entropy which were only recently calculated for higher-curvature gravity actions, which will be discussed in the next section.

A.2 Nonstationary Entropy

For several years it was unclear how to calculate SgravS_{\mathrm{grav}} for a nonstationary surface σ\sigma in a higher-curvature gravity theory, although some information was available using various methods such as field redefinitions and the GSL [84, 87, 88], holography [89, 90], and the Randall-Sundrum model [23].

A major breakthrough came when Lewkowycz and Maldacena [91] found a clever way to analytically continue the smoothed out n-sheeted replica trick in the context of calculating the holographic entanglement entropy (cf. section 6.5) in AdS/CFT. Their calculation involves performing the replica trick on the conformal boundary of the manifold, while requiring the interior to be a smooth solution to the equations of motion, exploiting the dynamical nature of gravity. One can then orbifold by the replica group ZnZ_{n} to find a manifold for which the n→1n\to 1 limit can be smoothly taken. This can be used to derive the Ryu-Takayanagi formula [64]1515 15 And presumably also the HRT formula [63], if one analytically continues using a complexified manifold. in the regime where the bulk theory is governed by the Einstein-Hilbert action.

Their calculation was quickly extended to determine the gravitational entropy functional SgravS_{\text{grav}} for higher-curvature theories. For quadratic gravity, see [92, 93, 94]; for Lovelock see [95, 96, 97]. In the more general case of f(Riemann) actions, SgravS_{\text{grav}} is given by the Dong entropy [93] But some ambiguities remain, related to the “splitting problem” [98, 99] (these references also make some inroads into the case where the action contains derivatives of the Riemann tensor).

Also, Faulkner, Lewkowycz and Maldacena showed how to include the 1-loop matter in the bulk using [24]; this corresponds to adding a bulk entanglement entropy term, thus replacing AA with SgenS_{\text{gen}} of the extremal surface, as done many times in this article.

Although these formulae were derived for holographic entanglement surfaces, they are consistent with the hypothesis that an entropy can be ascribed to more general surfaces. For example, the holographic entropy functional also seems to be the correct one to use when defining the GSL for linearized metric perturbations to Killing horizons, in any higher curvature gravity theory [55] (cf. [54, 53] for some special cases).

A.3 Example: 3+1 Dimensions

For example, in D=4D=4 semiclassical gravity coupled to free fields, the one loop corrections to the inverse of Newton’s constant 1/G1/G are quadratically divergent in ϵ\epsilon:

Δ1-loop​1G=fG​ϵ−2,\Delta_{\text{1-loop}}\frac{1}{G}=f_{G}\,\epsilon^{-2}, (53)

where the constant of proportionality fGf_{G} depends on the number and type of matter species. But there are also logarithmic divergences in the three parameters α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma associated with the quadratic gravity effective action [92]:

Ieff=∫d4​x​g​[R16​π​G+α​R2+β​(Rμ​ν)2+γ​(Rμ​ν​o​ξ)2]+Inonlocal.I_{\mathrm{eff}}=\int d^{4}x\,\sqrt{g}\left[\frac{R}{16\pi G}+\alpha R^{2}+\beta(R_{\mu\nu})^{2}+\gamma(R_{\mu\nu o\xi})^{2}\right]+I_{\mathrm{nonlocal}}. (54)

where, at one loop,

Δ​α1-loop\displaystyle\Delta\alpha_{\text{1-loop}} =fα​log⁡(ϵ)+gα;\displaystyle=f_{\alpha}\log(\epsilon)+g_{\alpha}; (55)
Δ​β1-loop\displaystyle\Delta\beta_{\text{1-loop}} =fβ​log⁡(ϵ)+gβ;\displaystyle=f_{\beta}\log(\epsilon)+g_{\beta}; (56)
Δ​γ1-loop\displaystyle\Delta\gamma_{\text{1-loop}} =fγ​log⁡(ϵ)+gγ.\displaystyle=f_{\gamma}\log(\epsilon)+g_{\gamma}. (57)

In general, coefficients of power law divergences such as fGf_{G} depend on the details of the renormalization scheme. But the coefficients of the log divergences fα,fβ,fγf_{\alpha},f_{\beta},f_{\gamma} are universal, depending only on the field theory [71].1616 16 In the special case of a CFT these parameters are determined by the central charges cc and aa, which determine the log divergences of the two conformally invariant contributions: Weyl squared (Cμ​ν​α​ξ)2(C_{\mu\nu\alpha\xi})^{2} and the Euler density Rμ​ν​α​ξ​Rπ​ρ​σ​τ​ϵμ​ν​π​ρ​ϵα​ξ​σ​τR_{\mu\nu\alpha\xi}R_{\pi\rho\sigma\tau}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\pi\rho}\epsilon^{\alpha\xi\sigma\tau} respectively. Although these two terms would be conformal if they were finite, their logarithmic dependence on ϵ\epsilon is a conformal anomaly; thus the partition function on curved spacetimes is not scale invariant. These log divergences appear because the dimension is even. (The finite piece of the 1-loop effective action is universal in odd dimensions, but in even dimensions this is true only up to local counterterms such as gα,gβ,gγg_{\alpha},g_{\beta},g_{\gamma}, since ϵ0\epsilon^{0} still counts as a power law!) The value of the ff coefficients for various spins in 4 dimensions are listed in [100, 101, 66], although there are certain issues with higher spin fields (3/23/2 and 22) which we will discuss in A.5.

Dimensional analysis reveals five possible covariant terms in the gravitational entropy density of σ\sigma due to α,β,γ\alpha,\,\beta,\,\gamma:

RRiiRi​ji​jKi​ai​Kj​ajKi​ja​Kai​j,R\,\,\,\qquad R_{i}^{\phantom{i}i}\qquad R_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}ij}\qquad K^{\phantom{i}i}_{i\phantom{i}a}K^{\phantom{j}j}_{j\phantom{j}a}\qquad K_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}a}K^{ij}_{\phantom{ij}a}, (58)

where Rμ​ν​ξ​oR_{\mu\nu\xi o} is the 4D Riemann tensor, Rμ​νR_{\mu\nu} the 4D Ricci tensor, RR is the 4D Ricci scalar, Ki​jaK_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}a} is the extrinsic curvature; also the indices i,ji,j represent directions parallel to σ\sigma, which are raised and lowered by qi​jq_{ij} (the metric restricted to σ\sigma), and aa represents an index normal to σ\sigma. The extrinsic curvature requires an aa index because σ\sigma is a codimension-2 surface, so that there are two remaining dimensions to bend into.

However, because there are only 3 possible terms in the action, only 3 linear combinations of these 5 terms can appear. The methods of A.2 show that the correct entropy functional is [89, 23, 92, 93, 94]

Sgrav=A4​G​ℏ+12​π​ℏ​∫σd2​x​g2​[α​R+β2​(Rii−Kii​a​Kj​aj)+γ⁡(Ri​ji​j−Ki​ja​Kai​j)]S_{\text{grav}}=\frac{A}{4G\hbar}+\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\int_{\sigma}d^{2}x\sqrt{{}^{2}g}\left[\alpha R+\frac{\beta}{2}\left(R_{i}^{\phantom{i}i}\!-\!K^{\phantom{i}ia}_{i}K^{\phantom{j}j}_{j\phantom{j}a}\right)+\gamma\left(R_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}ij}\!-\!K_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}a}K^{ij}_{\phantom{ij}a}\right)\right] (59)

Aside from the extrinsic curvature terms (which are ambiguous in the Noether charge formalism), this expression is the same as the Wald entropy (52). We may then define the generalized entropy as [102]

Sgen=⟨Sgrav⟩+SoutS_{\text{gen}}=\langle S_{\text{grav}}\rangle+S_{\text{out}} (60)

which in this case expands out to:

Sgen=limϵ→0[Sout(ϵ)+A4​G​(ϵ)​ℏ+14​π​ℏ∫σd2xg2×\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{gen}}=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\left[S_{\mathrm{out}}^{(\epsilon)}+\frac{A}{4G(\epsilon)\hbar}+\frac{1}{4\pi\hbar}\int_{\sigma}d^{2}x\sqrt{{}^{2}g}\,\times\phantom{MMMMM}\right.
(α(ϵ)R+β⁡(ϵ)2(Rii−Kii​aKj​aj)+γ(ϵ)(Ri​ji​j−Ki​jaKai​j))],\displaystyle\left.\left(\alpha(\epsilon)R+\frac{\beta(\epsilon)}{2}\left(R_{i}^{\phantom{i}i}-K^{\phantom{i}ia}_{i}K^{\phantom{j}j}_{j\phantom{j}a}\right)+\gamma(\epsilon)\left(R_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}ij}-K_{ij}^{\phantom{ij}a}K^{ij}_{\phantom{ij}a}\right)\right)\right], (61)

In the limit where ϵ\epsilon becomes small, the various dependences on ϵ\epsilon should cancel out, so that SgenS_{\mathrm{gen}} is independent of the choice of cutoff scale. Since the divergences in SoutS_{\text{out}} are local and proportional to the other terms in (61), it is manifest that there exists a choice of RG flow for the parameters G,α,β,γG,\alpha,\beta,\gamma for which SgenS_{\mathrm{gen}} becomes cutoff independent.

Thus the generalized entropy SgenS_{\text{gen}} is well-defined even though SoutS_{\text{out}} is cutoff dependent. As one shifts the cutoff, the entropy simply moves between the different terms.

A.4 Interpretation of Contact Terms

A crucial consistency condition is that the RG flow of the parameters in SgenS_{\text{gen}} (given by (61) at one loop in 3+1 dimensions) are in fact the same as for the corresponding parameter in the gravitational action (54).1717 17 For non-universal coefficients, the same regulator must of course be used on both sides.

Although the renormalization of the replica trick entropy automatically matches the renormalization of the gravitational action [103, 104], it is not so clear that the replica entropy can always be written as the sum of a horizon piece plus a statistical piece which is literally a von Neumann entropy −tr​(ρ​log⁡ρ)-\text{tr}(\rho\log\rho), as in (60). Thus if one e.g. imposes a regulator such as a brick wall (or a lattice) in which it is manifest that SgenS_{\text{gen}} has literally a statistical interpretation, and then compares to the replica trick with e.g. a smoothed out conical singularity, it is not a priori obvious that the RG flow of the two definitions of entropy will agree. The question is whether all terms in the replica entropy can be given a statistical interpretation.

For minimally coupled scalars and spinor fields, several calculations have shown an exact agreement between the geometric and statistical viewpoints [105, 69, 67, 106, 107, 108, 109] (modulo the K2K^{2} terms, whose coefficients were unknown in the 1990s but can now be determined and shown to agree by the methods described above).1818 18 But see [110] for an apparent discrepancy for scalars in odd dimensions, using a Pauli-Villars regulator.

There is an apparent mismatch [111, 102] between the replica entropy of non-minimally coupled scalars [67] and gauge fields [108], and their statistical entanglement entropy. Although the renormalization of the replica entropy automatically matches the renormalization of the gravitational action [103, 104], it is not so clear that this geometrical entropy can always be written as the sum of a horizon piece plus a statistical piece, as in (60). But these concerns can be resolved.

In the case of non-minimally coupled scalar fields whose Lagrangian includes the term ξ​ϕ2​R\xi\phi^{2}R, an extra “contact term” appears due to coupling to the conical singularity when performing the replica trick. This extra term is proportional to ξ​∫σ⟨ϕ2⟩\xi\int_{\sigma}\langle\phi^{2}\rangle. It contributes to the SgravS_{\text{grav}} (which in this case is equal to the Wald entropy (52)), and hence appears as an extra term in (61). It also contributes nontrivially to the RG flow of 1/G1/G, due to the multiplication of ϕ\phi at coincident points, restoring consistency [102].

In the case of Maxwell fields, there is also a contact term, which however cannot be explained by the addition of any term of the appropriate dimension to SgravS_{\text{grav}}.1919 19 By analogy to non-minimal scalar, one could try to add a term like Ai​Aj​g⟂i​jA_{i}A_{j}g^{ij}_{\perp}, where AiA_{i} is the gauge potential and g⟂i​jg^{ij}_{\perp} the inverse normal metric [102], but this is not a gauge-invariant combination. Nor does it appear in the holographic gravitational entropy [112] when derived by the Lewkowycz-Maldacena method [91]. Instead, the extra term arises from “edge modes” in the entanglement entropy due to the fact that boundary gauge symmetries are not gauged, and can be calculated by a path integral over the electric flux through the surface σ\sigma [113] (cf. [114]).2020 20 An alternative explanation [115] is that the contact term arises from the total derivative terms in the action. It has also been suggested [116, 117] that this would resolve a discrepancy between the field theoretical and holographic entropy calculations in 6 dimensions found by [90]. However, this interpretation departs from the usual principle that total derivatives may be dropped without consequence, and was argued against in [118].

A similar contact term involving gravitons can presumably be resolved in the same way, but here there are additional conceptual problems which we briefly explore next.

A.5 The Challenge of Higher Spin Fields

Defining the entanglement entropy for spin 3/2 and 2 fields is considerably trickier than for spins ≤1\leq 1.

First of all, as a result of their relationship to (super)gravity, they are only consistently defined when expanding around a gravitational background where the traceless part of the Ricci tensor vanishes (Einstein manifolds) [100].2121 21 In addition to these constraints, spin 3/2 fields require the cosmological constant to be negative or zero. A further issue (unique to fermionic gauge fields) is that when gauge-fixing the spin 3/2 field, one must take into account not only the Faddeev-Popov ghosts but also the Nielsen-Kallosh ghost [119, 120], in order to obtain the proper number of degrees of freedom [121]; see [122] for a correction of the spin 3/2 calculation in Ref. [111]. If the trace is nonzero, i.e., if there is a cosmological constant, the fields acquire an effective mass which must be included as in [123].2222 22 For this reason, among other errors, the R2R^{2} coefficient for gravitons or gravitinos found in [100, 101, 66] should not be used. This suggests that only some of the coefficients defined above are physically meaningful, namely those of the Weyl squared term and terms involving the Ricci scalar. As a result, the usual bulk replica trick method for defining the entanglement is suspect, since this is invalid off-shell [104].

A possibly related problem: In the case of gravitons, it is also necessary to decide on a covariant definition of the location of the surface σ\sigma. Choosing σ\sigma based on its coordinate location would make the results dependent on the choice of gauge.

In spite of these troublesome issues, some have ploughed ahead and calculated the fGf_{G} coefficient for linearized gravitons using a spin-2 gauge-fixed wave operator. Fursaev and Miele [124] found that the partition function of the replica manifold does not reduce in the limit β→2​π\beta\to 2\pi to the partition function of the smoothed out cone, which usually must agree [81]. Solodukhin [111, 125] also calculated fGf_{G} for the graviton, but his results appear to conflict with [124].

More ambitiously still, He et al. [126] calculated the entanglement entropy for the entire tower of higher-spin fields which appear in string theory, using an alternative definition of the replica trick on orbifold spacetimes where 1/n1/n is an integer. (For spin 3/2 and 2 their calculation agrees with that of [124].)

Notwithstanding the conceptual problems above, it should at least be possible to calculate the graviton entanglement entropy using the Lewkowycz-Maldacena method [91], in which the replica trick is performed on the boundary, and the equations of motion hold everywhere in the bulk. But this would only allow one to calculate the graviton entropy when σ\sigma is an extremal surface! It would not be sufficient for applications such as the QFC in which σ\sigma may be an arbitrary surface. Also, in order to derive the result of Faulkner et al. [24] for gravitons, one would need an independent bulk definition of the graviton entanglement entropy.

Thus, further exploration into the nature of entanglement entropy for gravitons and gravitinos seems warranted.
